title: DAC 2026: A Discussion of Who Owns the Intelligence Behind Tomorrow’s Chips and How to Make it Better - Semiwiki
gist: At a DAC 2026 panel organized by llmda.ai and moderated by SemiWiki's Daniel Nenni, IP providers (Alphacore, Arteris, Analog Bits) and EDA suppliers (Keysight, Siemens EDA, llmda.ai) debated the buy-versus-build question for agentic AI, with a stated goal of roughly 50% engineering productivity improvement. The recurring conclusions: open architecture across multi-vendor tools is mandatory, humans stay in the loop because errors require subtle insight, fabs bar new AI tools from advanced-process environments, and — per Nagesh Gupta citing Siemens/Wilson Research data — first-pass silicon success remains far below where it needs to be, making data accuracy rather than tooling the real bottleneck.

themes.theme: Agentic AI in the EDA flow

insights.claim: The industry is moving from simple documentation chatbots to agentic workflows capable of performing complex, multi-step tasks such as design creation, verification and library characterization, with these agents intended to enhance engineering productivity by roughly 50%.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: A ~50% productivity target is the number vendors are underwriting their AI roadmaps against — the benchmark to test in customer references before believing EDA seat-expansion or pricing-uplift stories.
insights.quote: These agents are intended to enhance engineering productivity by roughly 50%.

insights.claim: Amit Gupta of Siemens EDA identifies two distinct paths to the productivity goal: making existing EDA engines faster with AI, and adding an agentic orchestration layer that works alongside the engineer across the full design flow.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Separates incremental engine acceleration (defensible for incumbents) from the orchestration layer (contestable by startups) — the cleaner way to judge where value accrues.

insights.claim: Achieving agentic productivity gains requires an open architecture so tools from multiple vendors can work together, which is complex, and Siemens is committed to doing that work.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: An incumbent publicly committing to interoperability signals that walled-garden agent suites are not viable — reduces the lock-in premium in EDA valuations.
insights.locator: Amit pointed out that achieving this requires an open architecture

insights.claim: Michal Siwinski of Arteris expects the development of the orchestration layer to be an interesting place to watch, framing it as the contested new layer in the design stack.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Confirms multiple independent panelists converging on orchestration as the strategic control point — where M&A and startup funding should concentrate.
insights.locator: Michal mentioned the development of the orchestration layer

themes.theme: Buy versus build in the AI era

insights.claim: Amit Gupta observes a size-dependent split on make versus buy: larger companies are building some differentiating technology in-house while smaller and mid-size companies count on their supplier to deliver the whole solution.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Implies EDA vendors' agentic revenue skews toward the long tail of mid-size customers, while top-tier accounts internalize differentiation — a mix issue for pricing and TAM assumptions.

insights.claim: Daniel Nenni framed the panel with the historical observation that when he began his career in semiconductors there was no EDA industry — if you didn't build it, you didn't have it — and that buy-versus-build questions have persisted ever since.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: A reminder that the current AI build-versus-buy cycle rhymes with the original CAD-to-EDA commercialization — internal tools historically got absorbed by commercial vendors.
insights.quote: When Dan began his career in semiconductors there was no EDA industry. If you didn’t build it, you didn’t have it.
insights.locator: Dan kicked off the panel with a historical observation

insights.claim: Rusafa Shahreen of Alphacore characterizes AI tools interacting with humans as a 'build' strategy while the company simultaneously buys tools such as Cliosoft for IP and data management, illustrating that hybrid build-and-buy is the practical answer for IP providers.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Data-management tooling is being bought even by teams that build their own AI workflows — the stickier, more defensible revenue line.

insights.claim: Cliosoft has been purchased by Keysight, and Alphacore reports being very happy with the tool — a customer endorsement of the acquired asset delivered in front of Keysight's own panelist.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Evidence the Cliosoft acquisition is retaining and satisfying customers — supportive of Keysight's design-data-management franchise as an AI-era foundation layer.
insights.locator: Cliosoft has been purchased by Keysight

themes.theme: Humans in the loop and the limits of automation

insights.claim: Michal Siwinski sees humans remaining in the loop for the foreseeable future because the complexity of design data is high and finding errors can require very subtle insights.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Caps the near-term labor-substitution case for agentic EDA — productivity gains show up as throughput, not headcount reduction.

insights.claim: Siwinski argues that while standard models can be deployed at one level, maintaining differentiation and competitive edge requires some customization of the models, which itself drives continued human involvement.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Model customization is where competitive advantage is claimed to sit — favoring platforms that permit customer-specific tuning over one-size-fits-all agents.
insights.locator: to maintain differentiation and competitive edge

insights.claim: Rusafa Shahreen reports that Alphacore's IP delivery teams use AI tools such as Claude to increase the speed at which complex analog/mixed-signal designs can be examined and verified, while complete thorough validation of all deliverables remains a must-have.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: General-purpose frontier models are already inside IP-delivery workflows — evidence that horizontal AI vendors capture semiconductor spend without EDA-specific products.

insights.claim: Mahesh Tirupattur of Analog Bits summarizes the human-machine division of labor as 'AI is meant to accelerate good engineering,' pairing mandated high AI use at his company with engineering oversight.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: The adoption pattern that survives diligence: mandate usage but keep oversight — a template for judging whether a customer's AI deployment is real or theatrical.
insights.quote: AI is meant to accelerate good engineering.

themes.theme: Fab access as a structural constraint

insights.claim: Analog Bits designs on the most advanced processes and the fabs carefully guard access to that technology, so bringing new advanced AI tools into the fab isn't allowed — a hard constraint on deploying AI at the leading edge.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: An underappreciated ceiling on agentic EDA TAM: the most valuable leading-edge design environments are the hardest for new AI tools to enter, favoring vendors already inside the PDK trust boundary.
insights.quote: Bringing new, advanced AI tools into the fab isn’t allowed.

insights.claim: Tirupattur identifies digital model development as a good match for AI because many companies doing analog design have very little digital design know-how, and tools such as Claude can help develop the digital models required for new designs.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: A specific, near-term AI use case with a clear skills-gap driver — the kind of narrow wedge that gets adopted fastest in analog IP houses.
insights.locator: He explained that development of digital models

insights.claim: Analog Bits is enabling just about every AI device in some way, according to its CEO, positioning the analog IP supplier as a broadly embedded participant in AI silicon.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Analog IP is a quiet pick-and-shovel exposure to AI accelerator volumes across many customers rather than one.
insights.locator: Mahesh, who pointed out that Analog Bits is enabling

themes.theme: Data quality and trust as the AI foundation

insights.claim: Simon Rance argues that without high-quality data and meta-data that is carefully managed and governed it is difficult to have a successful AI deployment, and that Keysight's Cliosoft tool provides that trusted, secure data foundation for multi-vendor flows.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Reframes design-data management from back-office plumbing to an AI prerequisite — a re-rating argument for data-layer assets inside EDA portfolios.

insights.claim: Keysight positions itself around best-in-class multi-domain engineering tools such as multi-physics that must work with other vendors' tools in the flow, plus delivering the right context for the massive data driving the design process.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Keysight is playing best-of-breed-plus-data rather than full-flow suite — a different competitive posture than Siemens EDA's orchestration play.

insights.claim: The panel produced a spirited discussion on trust — what should be trusted and how an organization decides what to trust — with the author's conclusion that there is a critical place for quality human engineering in the process.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Trust criteria are unresolved industry-wide; whoever standardizes AI-output trust in chip design captures a governance chokepoint.
insights.locator: This was followed by a spirited discussion on overall trust

insights.claim: Arteris provides the underlying infrastructure for data communication across many applications and works with everyone, giving it a cross-industry vantage on how AI tooling is actually being adopted.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Arteris' neutral, everywhere position makes its adoption commentary a useful cross-check on vendor-specific AI claims.
insights.locator: Michal went on the explain that Arteris provides

insights.claim: Nagesh Gupta of llmda.ai frames the challenge everyone on the panel shares as the need for first-pass silicon success, arguing that efficiency without accuracy is not a winning strategy.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Reframes the whole AI-in-EDA value case around respin avoidance rather than speed — the metric with a direct, quantifiable dollar value.
insights.quote: efficiency without accuracy is not a winning strategy

insights.claim: Nagesh Gupta cited data from Siemens/Wilson Research showing first-pass silicon success isn't anywhere near as high as it needs to be, with projects often late as well.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: An industry-standard dataset showing the problem is unsolved — the quantitative basis for sizing the respin-avoidance market that agentic tools are chasing.
insights.locator: Nagesh cited data from Siemens/Wilson Research

insights.claim: Gupta's contrarian prescription is to focus not on the tools and the flow but on the data that drives the tools and the gaps in that data, because system specifications often drift out of sync leaving critical data no longer accurate.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: If specification drift is the root cause, spending on faster tools yields little — a screen for which AI-in-EDA investments actually address the binding constraint.
insights.locator: The approach here is not necessarily to focus on the tools

insights.claim: Organizational silos, geographic dispersion and poor processes between making insightful changes and broadly communicating them are identified as the contributors to specification drift, positioning it as an organizational rather than purely technical failure.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Tools that don't change organizational communication won't fix the root cause — a diligence question for any spec-verification vendor.

insights.claim: llmda.ai focuses on AI tools for embedded systems development and uses a comprehensive AI platform to ensure all forms of system specifications are verified to be accurate and tied to known good data.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Identifies a distinct niche — specification verification — adjacent to but not competing with mainstream EDA agent vendors.

themes.theme: Panel composition as a market map

insights.claim: The panel deliberately split into tool providers (Keysight, llmda.ai, Siemens EDA) and IP providers (Alphacore, Arteris, Analog Bits), with IP providers stating challenges and EDA suppliers responding — a structure that surfaces the supplier-customer tension in agentic AI adoption.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: A compact map of who supplies versus who consumes agentic AI in chip design — useful for tracing where AI budget flows in the semiconductor value chain.

insights.claim: The panel was organized by llmda.ai, described as one of the new agentic AI technology suppliers, and moderated by SemiWiki founder Daniel Nenni.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Worth discounting the framing: the sponsor's diagnosis — data accuracy as root cause — is also its product pitch.

insights.claim: Amit Gupta holds the dual role of Senior Vice President and GM of Siemens EDA's Solido Custom IC Division and Chief AI Strategy Officer, indicating Siemens has elevated AI strategy to a named executive function within EDA.
insights.speaker: Mike Gianfagna
insights.so_what: Executive-level AI ownership at a major EDA vendor signals AI is a P&L priority rather than a feature — expect it in product roadmaps and pricing.
insights.locator: Amit Gupta, Senior Vice President & GM
